explanations.explanation: That's the reason he gives: “for their hearts devise violence, and their lips declare trouble.” So it's what they plan inside and what comes out of their mouths. Wishing for their company is like asking to ride along with the guy who keeps setting off the smoke alarm on purpose. The teacher says skip it, friend.

Money is a fair thing to worry about, friend, but the teacher doesn't say it here. He says their hearts devise violence, and their lips declare trouble. That's the reason to skip their company. I think a shiny life on the outside can make us forget what's cooking on the inside.

explanations.answer: Their hearts are full of pride
explanations.explanation: Pride is a heavy thing to carry around, but it isn't what this verse names. The teacher says their hearts devise violence, and their lips declare trouble. So he points to what they plan and what they say. Hold on to that one, baker.

That's it, friend. Through knowledge the rooms are filled with “every precious and beautiful treasure.” Notice he says every one, not just a few. A house built wisely ends up with treasures in all its rooms, and it beats a house full of loose crumbs and good intentions.

explanations.answer: Tools for every kind of work
explanations.explanation: I get the thinking, because a house with good tools sounds handy. I own a whole bakery's worth, and I love them. But the teacher says the rooms are filled with “every precious and beautiful treasure.” He's talking about treasure, not toolboxes.

A full house of guests sounds lively, and I'd have to bake a LOT of cookies for that. But the teacher doesn't mention guests at all. He says knowledge fills the rooms with “every precious and beautiful treasure.” That's what the wise house holds.

Yes, friend. The teacher says, “Only with sound guidance should you wage war, and victory lies in a multitude of counselors.” One voice can miss something, so he points to many. Even a stamper like me asks around before moving the big oven. It's hard to out-guess a whole room of good advice.

Soldiers feel like the natural guess, I know. But the teacher says victory lies in a multitude of counselors. He's pointing to guidance, not numbers on the field. That's why he opens with “Only with sound guidance should you wage war.”

Weapons seem like they'd matter, friend, but the teacher puts his weight somewhere else. He says victory lies in a multitude of counselors. The first half of the verse sets it up: sound guidance comes first. So the winning pile is advice, not a pile of gear.

It's the opposite, friend. The teacher says the fool “does not open his mouth in the meeting place.” So he isn't holding the floor at all. I think a fool in that room looks a lot like a man staring hard at the meeting agenda and hoping nobody calls his name.

Right, baker. The teacher says wisdom is too high for a fool, and “he does not open his mouth in the meeting place.” So he has nothing to say there. Some people think a loud voice means wisdom, and this verse shows it doesn't always work that way.

That's what the teacher says: “a mocker is detestable to men.” Detestable is a strong word, and he picks it on purpose. A mocker might think he's the life of the party, but the verse says that's not how people see him. Laughing with folks is a gift, friend, and laughing at them is a different thing.
A mocker can sound clever for a minute, I'll give him that. But the teacher says “a mocker is detestable to men.” So the verdict isn't clever, it's detestable. That one sticks, friend.
It can look harmless, like just a joke or just a little eye roll. But the teacher says “a mocker is detestable to men.” Harmless isn't the word he picks. He says detestable, plain and strong.

True, friend. The teacher says, “If you faint in the day of distress, how small is your strength!” He's saying hard days show how much strength you really have. I think we all find out on a day like that what we're made of. Thankfully, he's already told us that wisdom makes a person strong (Proverbs 24:5).

Let me say it plain, baker. The teacher does say it: “If you faint in the day of distress, how small is your strength!” It's a gut check, and a loud one. I've had my own days when I wanted to flop over like dough that never rose, so I read this one slowly.

explanations.answer: The One who guards your life
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The teacher asks, “Does not the One who guards your life know?” He's answering the person who says they didn't know. The One who weighs hearts does know. He's saying nobody gets to hide behind not knowing, because that's one fact that can't be missed.

explanations.answer: The king who rules the land
explanations.explanation: A king knows plenty, I'll grant that. But in this verse, the teacher points higher. He asks, “does not He who weighs hearts consider it? Does not the One who guards your life know?” That's God he's pointing to, not a ruler of the land.

explanations.answer: The elders at the city gate
explanations.explanation: Elders at the gate know a lot of things, friend, but they're not who the teacher names here. He asks, “Does not the One who guards your life know?” He's pointing to the One who weighs hearts. That's a much bigger audience than a city gate.

That's the word, baker. The teacher asks, “Will He not repay a man according to his deeds?” It's the last of three questions in a row, and he leaves them hanging. Each one is a nudge that what we do matters. I think the questions land harder than a lecture would.

Wealth feels like a tempting guess, since people measure so much by it. But the teacher asks, “Will He not repay a man according to his deeds?” So it's what a man does, not what he owns. A full cookie jar doesn't change that, friend.

Family matters a lot, and I think about mine every day. But the teacher's question is about something else: “Will He not repay a man according to his deeds?” It's what each man does. That's the word to hold on to.

That's the point, friend. After the honey, the teacher says, “Know therefore that wisdom is sweet to your soul.” He's saying wisdom is good for you the way honey is good to your taste. The sweetness just goes deeper, down to the soul. Good thing the teacher doesn't make us pick between them.

Wealth is a fair guess, since people chase it hard. But the teacher says, “Know therefore that wisdom is sweet to your soul.” The honey is a picture for wisdom, not for money. It's a sweeter deal than it sounds.

Honor sounds nice, friend, and I'd take a little. But the teacher doesn't say honor is sweet to your soul. He says, “Know therefore that wisdom is sweet to your soul.” The honey points straight at wisdom.

True, baker. He says, “If you find it, there is a future for you, and your hope will never be cut off.” That's a promise worth holding onto. Compare it with the evil man, who has no future (Proverbs 24:20). Wisdom leaves your hope in one piece.

The teacher really does say it, friend: “If you find it, there is a future for you, and your hope will never be cut off.” It's a big promise about wisdom. I think it's one of the warmest lines in the whole passage. Read it twice if you need to.

That's it, baker. “For though a righteous man may fall seven times, he still gets up.” The verse doesn't say he never falls. It says he gets back up after each one. I know a thing or two about tipping over, and this verse gives me hope.

The verse doesn't go there, friend. The teacher warns the wicked man not to destroy a righteous man's resting place (Proverbs 24:15), but that's a warning. What it says about the righteous man is that he falls seven times and “still gets up.”

It's an easy guess after seven falls, I'll admit. Yet the teacher says the opposite: “he still gets up.” He also says if you find wisdom, your hope will never be cut off (Proverbs 24:14). So giving up isn't in the picture.

Yes, friend. The verse says, “but the wicked stumble in bad times.” Both groups can fall, but the difference is what happens next. The righteous man gets up, and in hard times the wicked stumble. It's the getting back up that sets them apart.

I see why it's tempting, since wicked people sometimes look like they're doing great. But the teacher says, “the wicked stumble in bad times.” That's why he tells us not to envy them. Their shine isn't the whole story.

Hiding makes sense as a guess, but it isn't the word here. The teacher says, “the wicked stumble in bad times.” He contrasts that with the righteous man, who falls and still gets up. Stumbling is the word.

explanations.answer: He would turn His wrath away from your enemy
explanations.explanation: That's what the verse says: “or the LORD will see and disapprove, and turn His wrath away from him.” The teacher says the LORD sees it, and He disapproves of the gloating. So a victory dance can backfire. I'd rather keep my feet still and my heart quiet.

explanations.answer: He would make you fall the very same way
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a neat match, friend, but the verse doesn't say it. The teacher says the LORD will see and disapprove, “and turn His wrath away from him.” The him is your enemy. Nothing is said about you falling the same way.

explanations.answer: He would raise your enemy up above you
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't say that, baker. It says the LORD will see and disapprove, “and turn His wrath away from him.” That's all it says happens to your enemy. Nothing there about raising him above you.
That's the first blank, friend. The teacher says, “For the evil man has no future.” It's the reason not to envy him. A big, flashy life that goes nowhere isn't worth wanting.

That's the second blank, baker. “The lamp of the wicked will be extinguished.” A lamp that goes out leaves a room dark, and that's a picture of the end of the wicked. It's a cold picture, which is why envying them makes no sense.
Rest makes sense as a word, but it doesn't fit the verse. The teacher says, “the evil man has no future.” Rest isn't the word he picks. A man with no future isn't missing a nap.

Lit is a close one, friend, since a lamp is the picture here. But the teacher says the lamp of the wicked “will be extinguished.” A lit lamp would be the opposite of what he says. The wicked lamp goes out.
Refilled is a hopeful guess, but it isn't there. The teacher says, “the lamp of the wicked will be extinguished.” Nobody comes by with a fresh jug of oil. The lamp simply goes out.

That's the one, friend. “My son, fear the LORD and the king, and do not associate with the rebellious.” The teacher puts those together in one breath. I think he's saying who you hang around with shapes where you end up. So choose your crowd the way you choose your dough, carefully.
Talkative folks get a bad rap sometimes, and I'll admit I can go on a while. But the teacher doesn't warn about them here. He says, “do not associate with the rebellious.” Chatting isn't the issue.
Having money isn't the problem in this verse, friend. The teacher says, “do not associate with the rebellious.” He names rebellion, not a bank account. So the wealthy aren't on his list.
It's the other way around, friend. The teacher says, “For they will bring sudden destruction.” Sudden means fast, with no slow warning. So the reason to steer clear is that it can hit fast.

Right, baker. The teacher says the rebellious “will bring sudden destruction.” Then he asks, “Who knows what ruin they can bring?” That's a big reason to pick your company carefully. I'd rather be around people who bring cookies.
